## The Weight Space View

Before moving to the full function space perspective, it is instructive to build intuition through a finite-dimensional parametric approach. The *weight space view* treats regression as Bayesian inference over a weight vector, and the structure of the resulting predictive distribution — once expressed in terms of inner products between inputs — naturally motivates the transition to Gaussian processes [@rasmussen_gaussian_2008; @mackay_introduction_1998].

We begin with a linear model of the form
$$
f(\vx) = \vx^\top \vw,
$$ {#eq-linear-model}
where $\vw \in \R^D$ is a weight vector. To make this more general, consider an expansion of basis functions [@bishop_pattern_2006]
$$
f(\vx) = \sum_{j=1}^{M} w_j \phi_j(\vx) = \vphi(\vx)^\top \vw,
$$ {#eq-basis-expansion}

where $\vphi(\vx) = [\phi_1(\vx), \ldots, \phi_M(\vx)]^\top$ is a vector of basis functions mapping the input to an $M$-dimensional feature space, with weights $\vw = [w_1, \ldots, w_M]^\top$. This is more general than the simple linear model, allowing non-linear relationships through the choice of basis functions $\phi_j(\cdot)$, without breaking linearity in the parameters $\vw$.

Given training data $\mathcal{D}$, our goal is to learn the weights $\vw$. Maximum likelihood (ML) estimation would yield a single point estimate $\hat{\vw}_{\text{ML}} = (\Phi^\top\Phi)^{-1}\Phi^\top\vy$ [@bishop_pattern_2006; @murphy_machine_2013], but this ignores the fact that many different weight vectors may explain the observed data equally well yet make very different predictions in unobserved regions — a manifestation of the bias-variance trade-off that becomes especially problematic with limited data and many parameters.

## Bayesian Linear Regression

### Prior and Likelihood

A Bayesian approach addresses this by placing a prior distribution over $\vw$, turning the problem into *Bayesian linear regression* [@bishop_pattern_2006; @gelman_bayesian_2025]. A natural choice is a zero-mean Gaussian prior:
$$
p(\vw) = \N(\vw \mid \vzero, \Sigma_p),
$$ {#eq-weight-prior}

where $\Sigma_p \in \R^{M \times M}$ is the prior covariance matrix. A common isotropic special case is $\Sigma_p = \sigma_w^2 \vI$, which gives i.i.d. Gaussian weights with variance $\sigma_w^2$ [@mackay_practical_1992].

Modelling each observation as $y_i = f(\vx_i) + \epsilon_i$ with independent noise $\epsilon_i \sim \N(0, \sigma_n^2)$, the likelihood for a single observation is
$$
p(y_i \mid \vx_i, \vw) = \N(y_i \mid \vphi(\vx_i)^\top \vw, \sigma_n^2).
$$ {#eq-likelihood}

Assuming independence across observations and conditioning on $\vw$, the joint likelihood over $\mathcal{D}$ is
$$
p(\vy \mid \vX, \vw) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} \N(y_i \mid \vphi(\vx_i)^\top \vw, \sigma_n^2).
$$ {#eq-likelihood-product}

Collecting observations into the *design matrix* $\Phi \in \R^{n \times M}$ with $\Phi_{ij} = \phi_j(\vx_i)$ [@rasmussen_gaussian_2008] (see [Appendix @sec-design-matrix] for the explicit construction), @eq-likelihood-product compresses to a single multivariate Gaussian:
$$
p(\vy \mid \vX, \vw) = \N(\vy \mid \Phi \vw, \sigma_n^2 \vI).
$$ {#eq-joint-likelihood}

### Posterior over Weights

Applying Bayes' theorem gives the posterior distribution over weights:
$$
p(\vw \mid \vX, \vy) = \frac{p(\vy \mid \vX, \vw) p(\vw)}{p(\vy \mid \vX)}.
$$ {#eq-bayes-theorem}

Because the Gaussian prior is conjugate to the Gaussian likelihood, the posterior is also Gaussian [@bernardo_bayesian_2000]. Completing the square in the joint exponent (see [Appendix @sec-completing-the-square] for the full derivation) gives the posterior covariance
$$
\Sigma_w = \left(\sigma_n^{-2}\Phi^\top\Phi + \Sigma_p^{-1}\right)^{-1},
$$ {#eq-posterior-cov}

and posterior mean
$$
\bar{\vw} = \sigma_n^{-2} \Sigma_w \Phi^\top \vy.
$$ {#eq-posterior-mean}

The posterior distribution over the weights is therefore
$$
p(\vw \mid \vX, \vy) = \N(\vw \mid \bar{\vw}, \Sigma_w).
$$ {#eq-posterior-weights}

## Predictive Distribution

This posterior distribution captures uncertainty about the weights given the observed data. We can use it to make predictions at a new input $\vx_*$ by marginalising over the weight posterior:
$$
p(f_* \mid \vx_*, \vX, \vy) = \int p(f_* \mid \vx_*, \vw) p(\vw \mid \vX, \vy) \, d\vw,
$$ {#eq-predictive-distribution}

where $f_* = f(\vx_*)$. Since $f(\vx_*) = \vphi(\vx_*)^\top \vw$ is a linear function of $\vw$, the marginal $p(f_* \mid \vx_*, \vX, \vy)$ is also Gaussian [@bishop_pattern_2006, Chapter 3]. Evaluating the integral in closed form gives the predictive mean and variance (see [Appendix @sec-predictive-variance] for the full derivation):

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{mean:} \quad & \E[f_* \mid \vx_*, \vX, \vy] = \vphi(\vx_*)^\top \bar{\vw}, \\
\text{variance:} \quad & \Var[f_* \mid \vx_*, \vX, \vy] = \vphi(\vx_*)^\top \Sigma_w \vphi(\vx_*) + \sigma_n^2.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-predictive-mean-var}

## From Weight Space to Function Space {#sec-weight-to-function-space}

The predictive distribution in @eq-predictive-mean-var is expressed in terms of the feature map $\vphi$. A critical observation is that $\vphi$ only ever appears through *inner products* of the form $\vphi(\vx)^\top \Sigma_p \vphi(\vx')$. This suggests defining a *kernel function* [@scholkopf_learning_2002; @rasmussen_gaussian_2008]
$$
k(\vx, \vx') = \vphi(\vx)^\top \Sigma_p \vphi(\vx'),
$$ {#eq-kernel-def}
which measures similarity between inputs in the feature space, weighted by the prior covariance $\Sigma_p$.

With this definition, collecting pairwise kernel evaluations over the training set into the *kernel matrix* $K \in \R^{n \times n}$ with $K_{ij} = k(\vx_i, \vx_j)$, and the vector of cross-covariances $\vk_* \in \R^n$ with $[\vk_*]_i = k(\vx_i, \vx_*)$, we can rewrite the predictive entirely in terms of the kernel. The key step is to reparametrize the posterior covariance $\Sigma_w = (\sigma_n^{-2}\Phi^\top\Phi + \Sigma_p^{-1})^{-1}$ using the matrix inversion lemma [@rasmussen_gaussian_2008, Equation A.9],
$$
(A + UCV)^{-1} = A^{-1} - A^{-1}U\bigl(C^{-1} + VA^{-1}U\bigr)^{-1}VA^{-1},
$$ {#eq-matrix-inversion-lemma}
setting $A = \Sigma_p^{-1}$, $U = \Phi^\top$, $C = \sigma_n^{-2}\vI$, $V = \Phi$, which yields the equivalent $n \times n$ expression:
$$
\Sigma_w = \Sigma_p - \Sigma_p\Phi^\top\bigl(\sigma_n^2\vI + \Phi\Sigma_p\Phi^\top\bigr)^{-1}\Phi\Sigma_p.
$$ {#eq-sigma-w-kernel}

In matrix form $K = \Phi\Sigma_p\Phi^\top$ and $\vk_* = \Phi\Sigma_p\vphi(\vx_*)$. Substituting @eq-sigma-w-kernel into the predictive mean $\E[f_*] = \sigma_n^{-2}\vphi(\vx_*)^\top\Sigma_w\Phi^\top\vy$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\E[f_*]
&= \sigma_n^{-2}\vphi(\vx_*)^\top\Sigma_p\Phi^\top\vy - \sigma_n^{-2}\vk_*^\top(K + \sigma_n^2\vI)^{-1}K\vy \\
&= \vk_*^\top\bigl[\sigma_n^{-2}\vI - \sigma_n^{-2}(K+\sigma_n^2\vI)^{-1}K\bigr]\vy \\
&= \vk_*^\top(K + \sigma_n^2\vI)^{-1}\vy,
\end{aligned}
$$
where the last step uses $\sigma_n^{-2}(K+\sigma_n^2\vI)^{-1}[(K+\sigma_n^2\vI)-K] = (K+\sigma_n^2\vI)^{-1}$. Substituting into the variance $\Var[f_*] = \vphi(\vx_*)^\top\Sigma_w\vphi(\vx_*) + \sigma_n^2$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\Var[f_*]
&= \vphi(\vx_*)^\top\Sigma_p\vphi(\vx_*) - \vk_*^\top(K+\sigma_n^2\vI)^{-1}\vk_* + \sigma_n^2 \\
&= k(\vx_*, \vx_*) - \vk_*^\top(K + \sigma_n^2\vI)^{-1}\vk_* + \sigma_n^2.
\end{aligned}
$$

The predictive distribution in terms of the kernel is therefore:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\E[f_* \mid \vx_*, \vX, \vy] &= \vk_*^\top (K + \sigma_n^2 \vI)^{-1} \vy, \\
\Var[f_* \mid \vx_*, \vX, \vy] &= k(\vx_*, \vx_*) - \vk_*^\top (K + \sigma_n^2 \vI)^{-1} \vk_* + \sigma_n^2.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-predictive-kernel}

Substituting these into the Gaussian predictive distribution from @eq-predictive-distribution gives:
$$
p(f_* \mid \vx_*, \vX, \vy) = \N\!\left(f_* \;\middle|\; \vk_*^\top(K + \sigma_n^2\vI)^{-1}\vy,\; k(\vx_*,\vx_*) - \vk_*^\top(K+\sigma_n^2\vI)^{-1}\vk_* + \sigma_n^2\right).
$$ {#eq-predictive-kernel-full}

Crucially, $\vphi$ has vanished entirely — the predictions depend only on kernel evaluations between data points. This means we are free to specify $k$ directly, without ever constructing an explicit feature map. In particular, if we allow $M \to \infty$ — infinitely many basis functions — and define $k$ to be the corresponding limiting inner product, the model becomes *non-parametric*: its effective complexity grows with the data rather than being fixed in advance [@williams_computing_1996; @mackay_introduction_1998]. Indeed, @williams_computing_1996 showed that a Bayesian neural network with an infinite number of hidden units and a Gaussian weight prior converges to a GP, making rigorous the connection between the weight-space and function-space views.

This is precisely the function-space perspective: instead of reasoning about an infinite weight vector $\vw$, we place a prior *directly over functions*, characterised entirely by $k$. The result is a Gaussian process.
